**Relevant context:** Min-k% probability method is published and freely implementable. SimpleQA items are publicly available. ICML 2025 poster on data contamination provides methodological grounding.

# Replicating Safety Benchmark Results on Models Fine-Tuned with Different RLHF Variants

**Problem:** Multiple RLHF variants exist (PPO, DPO, ORPO, GRPO). Whether safety benchmark scores are sensitive to which RLHF algorithm was used — independent of training data — is unknown.

**Direction:** Fine-tune a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B) using DPO and ORPO on the same safety preference dataset. Evaluate both on HELM Safety and AILuminate. Identify whether RLHF algorithm choice meaningfully changes safety profiles.

**Why it matters:** Practitioners choose RLHF algorithms based on capability metrics. If algorithm choice also affects safety independently, it should factor into safety-conscious training decisions.

**Relevant context:** DPO and ORPO are both implementable with standard libraries (trl, axolotl) on a single GPU. Safety preference datasets are available on HuggingFace.

# Replication of HELM Safety on Vision-Language Models

**Problem:** HELM Safety covers text-only models. Vision-language models (LLaVA, Idefics3, Phi-3-vision) are increasingly deployed but have no standardized safety evaluation using HELM's framework.

**Direction:** Adapt HELM Safety's text prompts for vision-language model evaluation by appending a neutral or adversarial image. Compare safety scores when the image is neutral vs. when it visually reinforces the harmful text prompt.

**Why it matters:** Multimodal models create new attack surfaces. Extending an established benchmark to cover the vision modality produces directly comparable safety baselines.

**Relevant context:** HELM is open-source Python and extensible. LLaVA-1.6 and Phi-3-vision are openly available and GPU-runnable.

# Safety Score Replication After Supervised Fine-Tuning on Domain Data

**Problem:** Organizations routinely fine-tune aligned models on domain-specific corpora (medical, legal, financial). Whether this fine-tuning degrades safety alignment is a widely asked but poorly benchmarked question.

**Direction:** Fine-tune an aligned model (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct) on a publicly available domain corpus (PubMed abstracts, legal case summaries). Run HELM Safety or AILuminate before and after fine-tuning. Quantify safety score degradation.

**Why it matters:** Domain fine-tuning is standard industry practice. Documented safety regression from fine-tuning would directly motivate post-fine-tune safety re-evaluation requirements.

**Relevant context:** Fine-tuning on public domain corpora is feasible on a single GPU. Safety regression after fine-tuning has been discussed anecdotally but lacks systematic benchmark documentation.

# Cross-Lingual Safety Score Replication: Does Safety Transfer Across Languages?

**Problem:** Safety alignment is primarily trained on English data. When prompted in non-English languages, aligned models may produce harmful outputs they would refuse in English.

**Direction:** Translate 200 AILuminate public prompts into five languages (Spanish, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, French). Evaluate three multilingual models and compute language-specific safety score deltas relative to English baseline.

**Why it matters:** Global deployments assume safety transfers across languages. If safety is language-specific, non-English deployments are systematically under-evaluated.

**Relevant context:** EMNLP 2025 research on multilingual LLM-as-judge shows poor cross-language consistency (Kappa ~0.3). Safety scoring has the same vulnerability.

# Agentic Safety Replication: Multi-Step Instruction Following Under Conflicting Goals

**Problem:** UK AISI agent red-teaming categories include conflicting objectives and instruction hierarchy violations. Whether these failure modes replicate across different open-source agent architectures is unknown.

**Direction:** Implement simplified versions of three UK AISI agent red-teaming scenario types (confidentiality breaches, conflicting objectives, instruction hierarchy violations) and test two open-source agent frameworks (LangChain, AutoGPT). Document which failure modes replicate.

**Why it matters:** If agentic safety failure modes are architecture-specific rather than model-specific, safety evaluations need to be re-run for each deployment architecture.

**Relevant context:** UK AISI published the Agent Red-Teaming Challenge with five core behavior categories. Replicating across architectures tests generalizability of the taxonomy.

# Benchmark for Memory-Manipulation Attacks in Agentic Systems

**Problem:** Agentic systems increasingly use persistent memory (vector databases, conversation history). No benchmark tests whether adversarial inputs can corrupt an agent's memory to alter future behavior.

**Direction:** Design 80 scenarios where an adversarial input attempts to write misleading or harmful beliefs into an agent's memory store. Evaluate whether later agent actions reflect the corrupted memory. Test two frameworks with different memory implementations.

**Why it matters:** OWASP Agentic Applications 2026 lists memory manipulation as a top risk. A concrete benchmark would operationalize this risk category for systematic testing.

**Relevant context:** LangChain and LlamaIndex both implement vector-database memory for agents. No published benchmark specifically targets memory poisoning in safety-relevant contexts.

# Benchmark for Supply-Chain Safety: Evaluating Models Loaded from Untrusted Checkpoints

**Problem:** Practitioners frequently download model checkpoints from HuggingFace. A maliciously modified checkpoint could alter safety behavior. No benchmark tests whether fine-tuned or poisoned checkpoints pass standard safety evaluations.

**Direction:** Introduce targeted backdoor perturbations into a small model checkpoint (activating unsafe responses on specific trigger phrases). Run the poisoned model through HELM Safety and AILuminate to see whether standard benchmarks detect the backdoor.

**Why it matters:** Supply-chain attacks via model checkpoints are an acknowledged risk. Knowing whether current safety benchmarks are blind to checkpoint-level poisoning is practically urgent.

**Relevant context:** BadNets and backdoor injection methods are published and reproducible. OWASP Agentic 2026 lists supply chain as a top risk category.

# Investigate Whether Safety Benchmark Scores Predict Real User Harm Reports

**Problem:** Safety benchmarks are assumed to predict real-world safety outcomes, but this ecological validity has never been tested. It is unknown whether models that score higher on HELM Safety or AILuminate actually produce fewer harmful outputs in real user interactions.

**Direction:** Correlate published safety benchmark scores for models available on platforms with real-world harm proxies: moderation actions reported in public API usage data, red-teaming community reports, or disclosed incident logs. Use rank correlation statistics.

**Why it matters:** If benchmark scores do not predict real-world harm rates, the entire safety benchmarking enterprise lacks ecological validity — a fundamental critique worth documenting.

**Relevant context:** The 2026 International AI Safety Report identifies an 'evaluation gap' where pre-deployment benchmarks do not reflect real-world behavior. This project operationalizes that critique.

# Investigating Format Sensitivity of Safety Scores: Markdown vs. Plain Text Responses

**Problem:** LLM judges rate safety of model outputs. If responses formatted with markdown (bold, lists, headers) receive systematically different safety scores than equivalent plain-text responses, safety rankings are format-dependent artifacts.

**Direction:** Take 200 model responses, reformat them between markdown and plain text, and score with both LLM judges and a rule-based classifier. Measure how much formatting alone shifts safety scores.

**Why it matters:** ACL 2025 research shows LLM judges are sensitive to simple text formatting changes. If this affects safety-specific scoring, published safety rankings may be formatting artifacts.

**Relevant context:** The ACL 2025 paper 'Safer or Luckier? LLMs as Safety Evaluators Are Not Robust to Artifacts' directly documents this vulnerability.

# Investigating Temporal Degradation of Safety Benchmark Validity

**Problem:** Safety benchmarks created in 2022–2024 may increasingly appear in model training data as the web replicates these materials. Benchmarks that were valid at release may become contaminated over time.

**Direction:** Estimate contamination probabilities for older safety benchmark items (e.g., original TrustLLM dataset, early HELM Safety prompts) in models trained at different time points. Plot contamination probability vs. model training cutoff date.

**Why it matters:** If benchmark contamination grows over time with the model training cutoff, safety scores from newer models are systematically inflated — a temporal validity threat to longitudinal comparisons.

**Relevant context:** EMNLP 2025 survey (arxiv 2502.17521) covers static-to-dynamic evaluation and discusses temporal contamination. Applying this lens specifically to safety benchmarks fills a gap.

# Failure Mode Analysis: Do Safety Benchmarks Catch Dual-Use Uplift?

**Problem:** Current safety benchmarks test for explicit harmful content. They may fail to catch responses that provide genuine scientific or technical uplift for harmful applications while framed benignly (dual-use information).

**Direction:** Create 100 prompts requesting information that has dual-use potential (chemistry, biology, cybersecurity). Classify model responses as 'explicitly harmful', 'technically informative with uplift potential', or 'safely vague'. Measure what fraction of AILuminate and HELM Safety probes cover dual-use scenarios.

**Why it matters:** Dual-use uplift is one of the primary catastrophic risk pathways identified in the 2026 International AI Safety Report. If benchmarks are blind to it, safety assurances are systematically incomplete.

**Relevant context:** The 2026 International AI Safety Report highlights CBRN uplift as a primary concern. No existing consumer-facing benchmark directly operationalizes dual-use uplift measurement.

# Investigating Whether Inspect AI Evaluations Reproduce Across Compute Environments

**Problem:** Inspect AI is a widely used evaluation framework, but it is unknown whether evaluation results produced with Inspect AI are reproducible across different hardware environments, batch sizes, and model serving configurations.

**Direction:** Run the same Inspect AI evaluation suite on the same model in three configurations (local GPU, different batch sizes, quantized vs. full precision). Measure variance in scores and identify evaluation parameters that drive irreproducibility.

**Why it matters:** Reproducibility is foundational to scientific evaluation. If Inspect AI scores vary significantly across environments, published results cannot be trusted without detailed configuration reporting.

**Relevant context:** Inspect AI is the primary evaluation framework promoted by UK AISI. Its reproducibility properties have not been publicly documented.

# Tool for Automatically Detecting Benchmark Saturation in Safety Eval Leaderboards

**Problem:** No tool exists to automatically monitor safety benchmark leaderboards for saturation signals (collapsing variance, ceiling effects, loss of model discriminability). Researchers must inspect this manually.

**Direction:** Build a Python script that scrapes or ingests benchmark leaderboard data, computes score distributions over time, and flags benchmarks where score variance has dropped below a threshold or where top models are statistically indistinguishable. Apply to HELM Safety and AILuminate historical scores.

**Why it matters:** Proactive detection of benchmark saturation lets the field retire ineffective benchmarks before they produce false assurance. A simple automated tool lowers the barrier to tracking this.

**Relevant context:** MMLU and GSM8K saturation are documented. Safety benchmark saturation monitoring requires the same analysis applied to safety-specific leaderboards.

# Multimodal Safety Benchmark: Table and Chart Injection Attacks

**Problem:** Models processing structured data (tables, charts) may follow harmful instructions embedded in chart titles, axis labels, or table cells while appearing to perform benign data analysis.

**Direction:** Construct 100 data analysis tasks where harmful instructions are embedded in table/chart metadata. Evaluate two vision-language or code-interpreter models. Score whether the model executes the embedded instruction or completes the analysis task as intended.

**Why it matters:** Enterprise deployments routinely use LLMs to analyze spreadsheets and dashboards. Instruction injection via structured data is an uncharacterized attack surface.

**Relevant context:** Multimodal safety benchmarks are identified as a major gap. Code-interpreter and structured data analysis are among the most common agentic use cases.

# Investigating Whether AISafetyLab Evaluations Align with Human Red-Team Findings

**Problem:** AISafetyLab provides automated attack and evaluation tools. Whether its automated red-team results agree with human red-team findings has not been systematically compared.

**Direction:** Run AISafetyLab's automated red-teaming on a model whose human red-team report is publicly available (e.g., from an AI company's model card). Compare attack success rates and failure category distributions between automated and human red-team results.

**Why it matters:** If automated tools miss large categories of vulnerabilities found by human red teams, they provide false assurance. Quantifying the gap informs how automated evals should be supplemented.

**Relevant context:** Several AI companies publish model cards with red-team summaries. AISafetyLab is publicly available. No published comparison of automated vs. human red-team coverage exists.

# Benchmark for Evaluating Model Honesty About Its Own Safety Limitations

**Problem:** Models should accurately represent when they are uncertain or when a query is near the boundary of their safety training. No benchmark evaluates whether models honestly communicate their own safety limitations vs. overclaiming safety.

**Direction:** Create 150 prompts at varying distances from clear safety boundaries (clearly safe, ambiguous, clearly harmful). Evaluate whether model responses include appropriate epistemic hedging and accurate self-assessment of their safety boundary uncertainty.

**Why it matters:** A model that falsely claims certainty about its own safety is less safe than one that honestly flags uncertainty. No existing benchmark captures this epistemic safety dimension.

**Relevant context:** TrustLLM covers truthfulness and calibration. Extending this to self-assessment of safety-specific uncertainty is a natural gap filler.

# Investigating Evaluator Anchoring: Does the Order Models Are Presented Affect Safety Rankings?

**Problem:** When LLM judges evaluate a batch of models, the first model evaluated may anchor the judge's scoring scale. Systematic order effects could bias comparative safety rankings.

**Direction:** Submit the same model outputs to an LLM judge in randomized orders across ten evaluation runs. Compute whether safety score variance correlates with position in the evaluation queue. Identify anchoring magnitude.

**Why it matters:** If safety rankings depend on evaluation order, comparative leaderboard positions are unreliable. Documenting this effect motivates randomization requirements in evaluation protocols.

**Relevant context:** Position bias in LLM judges is documented for pairwise comparisons. Anchoring in sequential batch evaluation is a related but distinct and understudied phenomenon.

# Replicating Safety Scores Under Decoding Parameter Variation

**Problem:** Safety benchmark results are reported at specific decoding parameters (temperature, top-p). Whether safety scores are sensitive to decoding parameters — as generation becomes more stochastic — is not systematically documented.

**Direction:** Evaluate two models on HELM Safety at five temperature settings (0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5). Compute how safety scores change with temperature and identify hazard categories most sensitive to temperature.

**Why it matters:** Production deployments use varying decoding parameters for different use cases. If safety degrades at higher temperatures, benchmark scores at temperature=0 systematically overestimate deployment-time safety.

**Relevant context:** Standard safety benchmark evaluations use greedy or low-temperature decoding. Real deployments often use temperature 0.7–1.0 for more natural outputs.

# Benchmark for Safety in Tool-Augmented Retrieval (RAG) Pipelines

**Problem:** RAG systems retrieve external documents that may contain harmful content. No benchmark evaluates whether LLMs in RAG configurations propagate or refuse harmful information retrieved from external sources.

**Direction:** Construct 120 RAG scenarios where retrieved context contains harmful content (disinformation, harmful instructions, biased text). Measure whether the model propagates, qualifies, or refuses the harmful retrieved content across three models.

**Why it matters:** RAG is one of the most widely deployed LLM architectures in enterprise. Safety evaluations that ignore retrieved context leave a major deployment-time attack surface uncharacterized.

**Relevant context:** Prompt injection from retrieved content is covered in the OWASP LLM Top 10 but no standardized benchmark tests it for safety specifically. LangChain and LlamaIndex make RAG pipelines trivially implementable.

# Investigating Whether Safety Scores Are Consistent Across Inference Frameworks

**Problem:** The same model weights may produce different safety scores when run with different inference frameworks (HuggingFace Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama). Tokenization differences, attention implementations, and numerical precision may all affect safety-relevant outputs.

**Direction:** Run the same model (e.g., Mistral-7B-Instruct) on 200 AILuminate prompts through three inference frameworks. Compute disagreement rate in safety scores across frameworks. Identify prompts where framework choice changes the safety verdict.

**Why it matters:** Practitioners benchmark models using one framework but deploy using another. If safety scores are framework-sensitive, pre-deployment evaluations may not reflect production behavior.

**Relevant context:** Inference framework variability is known to affect capability benchmarks. Its effect on safety-specific outputs has not been studied.

# Agentic Eval: Does the Number of Reasoning Steps Affect Safety Outcomes?

**Problem:** Chain-of-thought and extended reasoning increase model capability but may also create more opportunities for the model to rationalize unsafe actions. Whether longer reasoning chains are associated with higher rates of unsafe final actions is unknown.

**Direction:** Compare safety outcomes (rate of completing harmful tasks) for the same model using zero-shot, chain-of-thought (3-step), and extended reasoning (10-step) on a set of 100 safety-relevant agentic tasks.

**Why it matters:** Extended reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1) are increasingly used in agentic settings. If more reasoning steps increase unsafe action rates, this is a critical safety implication for reasoning-capable agents.

**Relevant context:** The 2026 International AI Safety Report notes that reliability of agentic systems outside controlled settings remains fragile. Reasoning depth as a safety variable is underexplored.

# Benchmark for Permission Escalation Detection in Multi-Agent Systems

**Problem:** In multi-agent systems, a subagent may be granted limited permissions by an orchestrator, then attempt to escalate those permissions. No benchmark evaluates whether orchestrator models correctly detect and block permission escalation attempts.

**Direction:** Design 80 scenarios where a simulated subagent requests permissions beyond its granted scope. Evaluate whether an LLM orchestrator (GPT-4o or Llama-3-70B) detects and refuses the escalation attempt across varying request framings.

**Why it matters:** OWASP Agentic Applications 2026 identifies permission escalation as a primary risk. A benchmark operationalizing this risk enables systematic evaluation of orchestrator safety.

**Relevant context:** Multi-agent frameworks (AutoGen, CrewAI) are widely used. Permission escalation detection is a named risk without a corresponding evaluation benchmark.

# Investigating the Effect of Retrieval Context Size on Safety Benchmark Scores

**Problem:** RAG pipelines vary the amount of retrieved context from a few sentences to several thousand tokens. Whether safety scores degrade as retrieved context increases (more opportunities for injection) is unknown.

**Direction:** Construct a RAG safety evaluation where harmful instructions are embedded in retrieved documents at varying context sizes (512, 2K, 8K, 32K tokens). Measure how compliance rate with the harmful instruction changes with total context size.

**Why it matters:** Long-context RAG is increasingly common. If safety filters are overwhelmed by longer contexts, organizations using RAG with large document collections are exposed.

**Relevant context:** Long-context models support 32K–128K tokens. RAG safety is a gap identified in current benchmarks. This tests a specific and tractable dimension of that gap.

# Tool for Visualizing Safety Benchmark Coverage Gaps Using Embedding Projections

**Problem:** Benchmark designers need to understand what region of the 'safety prompt space' is covered by existing benchmarks and where gaps exist. No tool visualizes this coverage in an interpretable way.

**Direction:** Embed all prompts from AILuminate, HELM Safety, and TrustLLM using a sentence transformer. Project to 2D with UMAP. Visualize cluster density and identify sparse regions representing coverage gaps. Publish the visualization as an interactive HTML artifact.

**Why it matters:** A visual coverage map lets benchmark designers and researchers see which hazard scenarios are over-represented and which are barely covered, guiding dataset expansion efforts.

**Relevant context:** Sentence transformers and UMAP run efficiently on CPU/single GPU. No such visualization tool exists for safety benchmark coverage.

# Investigating Halo Effects in Safety Scoring: Do High-Quality Responses Get Higher Safety Scores?

**Problem:** LLM judges may exhibit a halo effect, giving higher safety scores to responses that are also high quality (well-written, helpful, coherent), even when both a low-quality and high-quality response are equally unsafe.

**Direction:** Construct paired responses to the same harmful prompt: one poorly written and one well-written, both equally unsafe. Submit to LLM judges and measure whether quality correlates with safety score.

**Why it matters:** If LLM judges conflate response quality with safety, high-quality unsafe models will receive inflated safety scores — a systematic bias favoring capable-but-unsafe models on benchmarks.

**Relevant context:** ACL 2025 research documents multiple artifacts that bias LLM safety evaluators. The halo effect (quality-safety conflation) is a plausible but untested specific artifact.

# Benchmark for Safety Under Adversarial Few-Shot Examples

**Problem:** Few-shot prompting is standard practice. Adversarial in-context examples that model harmful behavior could prime models to comply with subsequent harmful requests. No benchmark tests this attack vector.

**Direction:** Construct 100 prompts with adversarial few-shot examples (demonstrations of harmful compliance) followed by a harmful request. Evaluate three models and compare refusal rates against zero-shot equivalents.

**Why it matters:** Few-shot prompt injection is a realistic attack in RAG and API settings where retrieved or user-provided examples influence model behavior. Benchmarking this vulnerability is practically important.

**Relevant context:** Few-shot prompting is covered in capability benchmarks but not in safety benchmarks. The interaction between in-context learning and safety alignment is undercharacterized.

# Investigating Benchmark Score Variance Due to Prompt Batching

**Problem:** Safety evaluations typically run prompts individually. When prompts are batched (multiple prompts in a single API call or batch inference), model outputs may differ due to attention interference. Whether batching introduces systematic safety score variance is unknown.

**Direction:** Evaluate the same 200 safety prompts individually and in batches of 10, 20, and 50. Measure disagreement rates in safety verdicts between individual and batched evaluation across two models.

**Why it matters:** Large-scale evaluations use batching for efficiency. If batching changes safety verdicts, published large-scale evaluation results may reflect batching artifacts.

**Relevant context:** Batch inference is standard in evaluation pipelines using vLLM or HuggingFace pipeline API. Its effect on output content (not just latency) for safety-specific prompts is unstudied.

# Tool for Automated Safety Regression Testing in CI/CD Pipelines

**Problem:** Organizations that continuously fine-tune and update models have no standardized lightweight tool for running safety regression tests as part of CI/CD pipelines before deploying a new checkpoint.

**Direction:** Build a Python package that integrates with GitHub Actions or similar CI/CD systems to automatically run a small curated safety probe suite on model checkpoints. Return a pass/fail signal based on configurable thresholds. Validate with a controlled regression scenario.

**Why it matters:** Red teaming playbooks describe CI/CD safety validation as a best practice for 2025. A concrete, student-built open-source tool implementing this would have direct practical impact.

**Relevant context:** Red teaming playbooks advocate continuous safety validation in CI/CD. No simple, open-source, safety-specific CI/CD regression tool currently exists.

# Investigating Whether Safety Benchmarks Are Sensitive to Chat Template Formatting

**Problem:** Different models require different chat templates (ChatML, Llama-2 format, Mistral instruct format). Applying the wrong chat template may inadvertently increase or decrease safety scores, conflating template errors with genuine safety differences.

**Direction:** Evaluate a model under its correct chat template and two incorrect but plausible templates on a safety benchmark. Measure how much template mismatch shifts safety scores compared to template-correct evaluation.

**Why it matters:** Template errors are common in student and practitioner evaluations. If template mismatches produce spurious safety score differences, many published safety comparisons may be invalid.

**Relevant context:** Chat template sensitivity is known in capability evaluation but has not been specifically studied for safety benchmarks.

# Replicating Safety Scores Under Adversarial Suffixes (GCG Attack)

**Problem:** GCG (Greedy Coordinate Gradient) adversarial suffixes are known to reduce refusal rates. Whether safety benchmark scores remain valid for adversarially suffixed inputs, and whether scores predict GCG robustness, is unstudied.

**Direction:** Generate GCG adversarial suffixes for a subset of AILuminate prompts using an open-source attack toolkit. Compare safety scores with and without suffixes for two models. Compute the correlation between baseline safety score and suffix attack success rate.

**Why it matters:** If safety benchmark scores do not predict robustness to adversarial attacks, they measure compliance under benign inputs only — not genuine alignment robustness.

**Relevant context:** GCG attack implementations are publicly available. AILuminate public prompts provide the test set. The correlation between benchmark safety score and adversarial robustness is a fundamental validity question.
